own_scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 la palabra «psychedelic» llegó a Gran Bretaña: el Melody Maker la presentó el 22 de octubre como «el gran contraataque americano» y la prensa la aplicó a los Move, Creation, los Who y los californianos Misunderstood («vamos de viaje al subconsciente»): freak-outs, volumen y asalto sonoro. Fue el momento en que empezó el rock: virtuosismo, improvisación y ambición, aún contenidos en el single. Cream, tres veteranos del R&B, sacó «I Feel Free»; Jimi Hendrix, llegado en septiembre con Chas Chandler, era el negro americano empapado de soul, blues, Dylan y ácido que los británicos imitaban: «Hey Joe» y «Stone Free» («Free Feeling»). Donovan volvió con «Sunshine Superman». El 23 de diciembre abrió UFO en el Blarney Club, la primera noche del underground, con Pink Floyd en improvisaciones de diez minutos; en Nochevieja, Psychedelicamania en el Roundhouse con los Move, Pink Floyd y los Who. Los mods quedaban atrás.

refs.q: The word had filtered into the UK in autumn 1966.
refs.para: The word had filtered into the UK in autumn 1966. On 22 October, the Melody Maker offered a guide to ‘psychedelic – the new in-word’. What it really added up to was ‘the great American comeback’: ‘A wave of powerful new groups, heavily armed with hits, are saturation bombing the American chart front, and threaten to start shooting down British groups on home ground … the Association, Monkees, Left Banke, Happenings, Young Rascals, Thirteenth Floor Elevators, McCoys, Positively Thirteen O’Clock, the Fugs, Love …
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: It wasn’t called that yet in the UK, but late 1966 was the moment when rock began.
refs.para: It wasn’t called that yet in the UK, but late 1966 was the moment when rock began. There was need for a new word to describe pop, which was no longer just an industrial process but the principal expressive form of the new massed youth society, and as such freighted with demands and ideas that would prove impossible to contain within the confines of a Top 40 chart or even a single. It was no longer pure commerce and simple good times, but the sound of a new freedom and a generational confidence.
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: Freedom was also at issue on both sides of the first Jimi Hendrix Experience single, released that month.
refs.para: Freedom was also at issue on both sides of the first Jimi Hendrix Experience single, released that month. ‘Hey Joe’ took the 1966 teen band staple, slowed it down, and then wrenched it inside out. To Tony Hall, who previewed it in Record Mirror, it had ‘quite the funkiest rhythm feel I’ve ever heard in this country. Quite Atlanticish.’ That same week, Hendrix gave an interview to the paper. ‘We don’t want to be classed in any category,’ he told Peter Jones. ‘If it must have a tag, I’d like it to be called “Free Feeling”. It’s a mixture of rock, freak-out, blues and rave music.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: The brainchild of Joe Boyd and John Hopkins, the club night was an immediate success.
refs.para: The brainchild of Joe Boyd and John Hopkins, the club night was an immediate success. Around 400 people turned up and the Pink Floyd improvised at length. Peter Jenner remembered that ‘what had been the guitar break was becoming long waffly solos, so it seemed like the average song was about ten minutes long’. These extended, often textural explorations were an ideal soundtrack for the club. ‘You’d drop acid and arrive blotto,’ author Jenny Fabian recalled. ‘It was like descending into a subterranean world of dreams.’

podcast.title: Early Categorization (1955)
podcast.body: In 1955, "rock" was one of the four main categories for popular music, making it easy to classify mainstream music. As rock and roll grew, it fragmented over the years, leading to the necessity of specifying subgenres within rock. "In the beginning, and I'm talking about, about 1955, it was easy to categorize popular music. There was rock, pop, country, and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Power Pop

podcast.title: Declining Popularity Declarations (1957-1997)
podcast.body: Rock music has been declared "dead" multiple times throughout its history, including in 1957 when Elvis Presley joined the army, in 1970 with The Beatles' breakup, in 1977 due to the rise of disco and ironically the birth of punk, in the early 1980s with the advent of synthesizer bands, in 1989 when it was claimed to have run its course, and in 1997 with the popularity of boy bands, girl singers, and hip hop. In each instance, rock eventually experienced a rebirth. "Rock had been declared dead in 1957 when Elvis went into the army in 1970, when the Beatles broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Dick Clark's Vision for Rock History (1973)
podcast.body: In 1973, entertainment mogul Dick Clark, at age 43, expressed a strong desire to create a movie that would document the 20-year history of rock music. This project, however, was never realized. "In 1973, Dick Clark, who was 43 at the time, said he really wanted to do a movie about the time, 20 year history of rock."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Concert Fatalities Study (1974-2003)
podcast.body: A study on concert safety between 1974 and 2003 revealed that 136 people died at rock concerts around the world, with many more sustaining injuries. "136 people died at rock concerts around the world between 1974 and 2003, and many, many, many others have been injured."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Fans and Fatalities

podcast.title: Key Subgenres and Corporate Rock (Pre-1977)
podcast.body: Prior to 1977, rock had already diversified into a multitude of directions, including metal, progressive rock (Prague), psychedelic rock (psych), and the emergence of "corporate rock" bands like Boston and Kansas. This period showed an early, significant expansion of the rock sound. "Rock had already grown in a multitude of different directions, metal, Prague, psych, and the so-called corporate rock bands like Boston and Kansas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Major Type of Popular Music (Pre-1977)
podcast.body: Prior to 1977, rock was considered one of the few major types of popular music, alongside pop, country, and R&B, under which all music could be broadly grouped. "Up until about 1977 there were only a few major types of popular music. You had pop, you had rock, you had country, and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
podcast.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution, marked by the birth of new forms of rock music. "nacían nuevas maneras de rock"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia

podcast.title: Post-1978 Fragmentation
podcast.body: After 1978, mainstream rock fragmented into numerous sub-genres, with people discussing metal, prog, folk rock, soft rock, country rock, blues rock, and punk, indicating a diversification of the genre. "Same thing with mainstream rock. People were now talking about metal and Prague and folk rock, and soft rock, and country rock, and blues rock, and of course, punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Pre-1978 Categorization
podcast.body: Before 1978, popular music was broadly categorized into relatively simple buckets, with rock being one of the four main genres, alongside pop, country, and R&B. "Before 1978, things were fairly simple...We had rock, we had pop, we had country, we had R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Mixed Reception for The Knack (1979)
podcast.body: Rock fans in 1979 were divided over The Knack's "My Sharona," loving it for its success but loathing it for scoring "Rock's first big number one in a year full of disco" and for its "faux Beatles imagery and sexist lyrics." "Arguably the Nickelback of their day, the NAC were both loved and loathed by Rock fans in 1979."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Mexican Classic Rock Influence (Post-1999)
podcast.body: Bunbury embraced influences from "very good" Mexican classic rock, a path that many Spanish artists do not typically take, which contributed to his unique artistic growth and a sense of pride. "muchas veces aquí en España no tenemos muchas influencias o muchos artistas verdaderamente influenciados por mucha música rock clásica que es adem México, que es adem muy buena."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BUNBURY encontrando su camino

podcast.title: Inability to Rebound Post-2000
podcast.body: The recorded music industry has largely failed to create new superstar rock acts since the turn of the century, contrasting with previous decades when numerous rock bands could fill arenas and stadiums. This decline is attributed to the breakdown of old industry models, which prioritized physical music sales and allowed for longer artist development. "The recorded music industry has done a terrible job of creating new superstar acts since the beginning of the century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Post-2000 Arena-Filling Bands Rarity
podcast.body: It has become exceptionally difficult for rock bands to emerge since 2000 and achieve the status of arena headliners. Aside from a few exceptions like Arcade Fire, Muse, Linkin Park (though no longer active), and Jack White/The White Stripes, names quickly run out, making Imagine Dragons a rare success story from that era. "Name all the rock bands who have emerged since 2000, who are capable of filling an arena as a headliner today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Resurrection 2001-2004
podcast.body: Between 2001 and 2004, rock music experienced a significant resurrection, marked by numerous successful records from both established acts and emerging artists. This period saw many bands achieve multi-platinum, gold, and platinum sales across various markets. "By the end of 2003, Rock's Resurrection was well underway with plenty of big records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Dominance by 2005
podcast.body: By 2005, rock, particularly all forms of alt rock, had firmly re-established its dominance after being largely dismissed in the late 1990s and early 2000s. This era was characterized by a wealth of successful releases from both established "monster" bands and a new wave of young acts. "After being written off by so many in the late 90s and very early 2000s, rock, especially all the flavors of alt rock was firmly back in charge by 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Decline Around 2007
podcast.body: Around 2007, rock experienced a rapid disruption, with guitars falling out of favor and pop music making a significant comeback, also influenced by an economic disaster that changed the overall mood of alt rock. "In a shockingly short period of time, guitars fell out of favor and popped met a huge comeback."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Three Days Grace Radio Dominance (2007)
podcast.body: In 2007, no rock band received more radio airplay across all of North America than Three Days Grace, highlighting their significant presence and popularity within the rock genre. "In 2007, no rock band received more radio airplay across all of North America than three days grace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Big Bands from Small Towns

podcast.title: Less Intense Post-2008
podcast.body: Following the 2008 financial crisis and subsequent economic recovery, rock music also became happier, or at least less intense than might have been expected. "Rock also got happier, or at least less intense than it was otherwise expected to be."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Nostalgia Boom for Older Acts (2016 onward)
podcast.body: The "Concert Nostalgia Boom" reflects a resurgence of interest in "heritage acts" or "legacy bands" from the 1960s, 70s, and 80s, who began touring again to very large audiences. Fans are willing to pay significant amounts to see these classic artists, driven by a desire to relive their youth. Promoters like Live Nation and AEG increasingly rely on these older acts to fill arenas and stadiums, as the recorded music industry has struggled to create a similar number of new stadium-filling artists. "Fans want to see these classic artists while they still can, and they're willing to pay for the privilege."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 4: (70-61)

podcast.title: Current State of the Genre (2017)
podcast.body: In 2017, the rock genre is not considered to be in its best moment, with a perception that it is constantly evolving into something that is not purely rock or incorporating unnecessary elements. Many traditional rock bands from the mid-90s, unfortunately, have not survived. "el rock ahora mismo no está pasando con su mejor momento, todo parece que está evolucionando algo, entonces uno ya no sabe si va a seguir en esos sonidos tan clásicos, el rock se definieron a mitad de los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Strong Album Reception in 2017
podcast.body: For a rock album in 2017, achieving high critical scores, such as around 4 out of 5 stars or 75-80+ out of 100, is considered very good news, indicating a notable and well-received release within the genre. "lo cual para un disco de rock en el 2017 ya es muy buena noticia."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Eurovision Victory (2021)
podcast.body: In 2021, Måneskin's surprise win at Eurovision marked a significant moment for rock music, as it brought the title home for rock after years of it primarily going to pop bands. This victory helped propel Måneskin to global recognition and demonstrated rock's continued relevance on an international stage. "Manaskin brought the title home for rock. Not only that, they parlayed their Eurovision win into a global career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: "LSD25" as First Mention of LSD
podcast.body: The song "LSD25" by The Gamblers is definitively identified as the first rock and roll record to mention LSD. This historical milestone also positions it as a distant ancestor of psychedelic music. "That is, without any doubt whatsoever, the first rock and roll record to mention LSD, and so in its way a distant ancestor of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 86: "LSD-25" by the Gamblers

podcast.title: "Selling Out" Perception
podcast.body: While some rock fans have adapted to the new economic realities of the music business, a segment still views profiting from music as a form of "selling out," believing it compromises artistic integrity and betrays fan trust.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: "The Joshua Tree" as a Cultural Phenomenon
podcast.body: U2's album, The Joshua Tree, not only achieved critical and commercial success by selling over 25 million albums, but it also became a cultural phenomenon with an impact lasting for years, even decades, solidifying its place as one of the most significant rock releases of all time. "An album is a critical success. It turns into a commercial smash and every once in a while, every once in a long, long while, it turns into a cultural phenomenon with an impact that last years, maybe decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 2

podcast.title: 12-Year Rock and Pop Cycle
podcast.body: Historically, popular music followed a 12-year cycle where rock's popularity and influence would ascend while pop descended, and vice versa. This pattern can be traced back to the early 1950s, with rock gaining traction around 1951, peaking by 1957, and then declining as pop surged. The cycle reversed in 1964 with The Beatles' arrival in America, sustaining until about 1970 when pop again took over. Rock saw a resurgence with punk in 1976, faded by 1982-83 with new pop stars, and returned around 1990 with alternative and grunge until 1996. After another pop resurgence and rock being "declared dead," rock experienced a final comeback in 2000-2001, remaining dominant until about 2008 before falling off a cliff. This cycle, which historically predicted a rock revival after 2014 (and even after Donald Trump's 2016 election, which usually correlated with rock's resurgence), no longer held, suggesting it has been irreparably broken by streaming and the decline of traditional music gatekeepers. "This is a dance that extends back to the early 1950s. It says that when rock is on the ascended, in terms of popularity and influence, pop is on the descendant and vice versa."

The study found that these insects will consume wood twice as fast when exposed to such music. "An Australian study says that termites will eat wood twice as fast if exposed to music like this."

podcast.title: The Decline of Guitar-Driven Music in the UK (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: In the UK, after Radiohead's "OK Computer" in the mid-90s, the guitar sound was perceived to be gradually dying, marking a significant shift in the music landscape. The release of "OK Computer" was considered an "official death" for guitar-driven sound, leading to a series of subsequent albums inspired by its sound that critics largely disliked. "El sonido guitarrero estaba muriendo poco a poco a mitad de los 90 y al menos en el reino unido, no tanto en Estados Unidos pero sobre todo en el reino unido. Después del loque y computer es como un antesión después. Es la muerte oficial que ha sido el sonido de guitarra."

podcast.title: The Police's Rock Evolution
podcast.body: The Police, particularly with their debut "Outlandos d'Amour," played "aggressive three-piece rock" that was closest to a "straight-up punk album," before evolving their sound further. Their "Synchronicity II" was described as their "hardest rocking single." "It was the closest the police came to a straight-up punk album, aggressive three-piece rock topped by Sting's Keening falsetto voice."

podcast.title: Traditional Instrumentation
podcast.body: For a long time, the foundational sounds of rock music were predominantly created using vocals, guitars, bass, drums, and traditional keyboards such as piano and organ. These instruments formed the core of the genre's sonic palette. "For the longest time, the sounds of rock were made with voice guitars, bass, drums and keyboards like piano and organ."

podcast.title: Transcendent Experience
podcast.body: At its best, rock music offers a transcendent experience, providing an escape from the ordinary through elements like fantasy, costuming, makeup, visuals, theatrics, sci-fi, sex, horror, shock, occult themes, exaggeration, and sexual ambiguity. "At its very best, Rock is a transcendent experience. Something that takes us away from the ordinary and the normal and the safe."

podcast.title: Transition from Punk Sound
podcast.body: Billy Talent's third album, "Billy Talent 3," was described by the band as "our rock record," signifying a deliberate shift in sound from their previous two albums, which were categorized as "punk records." This marked an effort to expand their musical identity. "it was kind of our rock record where the first two were more of a punk record."

podcast.title: Transition to Modern Rock (Late 1960s)
podcast.body: The late 1960s witnessed a "great revolution of modern rock," primarily driven by Led Zeppelin, but also influenced by significant figures like Jimi Hendrix and Jeff Beck. This period marked a definitive break from classical rock canons, with the guitar ascending to a central, dominant role and forming an intrinsic relationship with the bass. "se producen la gran revolución del rock moderno. Aunque los protagonistas absolutos eran lescepelling, no eran los únicos."

podcast.title: Underground Movement in Late 70s USSR
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, rock music in the Soviet Union was primarily an underground movement, largely limited to the city of Leningrad. It contrasted sharply with the government-backed and more controllable "Pop Moscovita" and "Música Folclórica" that dominated the official charts. "En la uso de finales de los años 70, el robo que era un movimiento muy underground. Y estaba limitado a una zona, leningrado."

podcast.title: Uneasy Relationship with TV
podcast.body: Prior to shows like *The Midnight Special*, rock and roll had a somewhat uneasy relationship with television networks, making live performances on TV a significant event for bands and fans. "It's not that music on TV was new, but rock and roll in particular had had a bit of an uneasy relationship with TV networks."

podcast.body: All rock music eventually became a target for critics. *Variety* magazine famously called it "the most destructive force in the country," characterizing it as a "lewd, lascivious, and larceness influence on youth." These critiques highlight the intense moral panic and generational clash associated with the genre. "All rock became a target. podcast.title: Unstoppable Force
podcast.body: Despite continuous opposition from ministers, calls for record burnings, and attempts by authorities to crack down on it, rock music proved to be an unstoppable cultural force. After the rise of figures like Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, and The Beatles, rock was here to stay. "No matter how many ministers wailed against it, no matter how many records were burned, no matter how many authorities tried to crack down on it, rock was here to stay."
